acting president of the council. - mr. speaker, the house! i had the opportunity to present a preliminary analysis of the first european semester a few months ago, but the results and the scale of the process are still unknown. the final assessment of the extent to which the present regime is living up to its expectations will only be possible once the national parliaments have finally adopted the draft budgets for next year. the whole idea of the european semester is to involve national decision-makers more in the process of implementing the priorities of the european union's growth and development. hence, the whole system initiated by the european commission in the annual growth survey, which sets out priorities which are then translated into individual recommendations for the member states, will only be effective if this information, these priorities, are properly communicated to national parliaments and national parliaments take all these aspects into account when adopting the national budget. we have some experience after less than a year of this process. today, the annual growth survey was presented at the ecofin council and here is the first conclusion that we have drawn together with the commission. the first conclusion is that the process of discussion and decision-making that has been designed so far has been too condensed in time. thus, unlike the first, this draft annual growth survey was presented more than a month in advance of the previous one, giving the council and other institutions, including the member states, more time to analyse and prepare their quasi-national responses to the challenges identified by the european commission. the time constraint was one of the first elements that emerged during the implementation of this process. commissioner rehn also presented two more draft regulations today during ecofin, which will improve the existing system that is currently being implemented. they increase the scrutiny, by the european commission in particular, of the procedure - i would prefer not to call it the budgetary procedure - for communicating the union's priorities and the way forward to national parliaments. these two regulations are limited for now to the euro area as the group of countries that currently have the greatest obligations in this area and the greatest challenge to improve the economic situation in the european union, to improve the situation of public finances. furthermore, what is very interesting and i think this is a very good initiative on the part of the european commission in both regulations there are clear indications as to the involvement of the european parliament in the process of discussing these priorities and how they are implemented by the member states. under the current system, it is not clear what this discussion is supposed to be about. both draft regulations clearly indicate that the relevant committees of the european parliament may invite representatives of the member states as well as the european commission to the debate. the european parliament will be able to discuss both the recommendations for individual member states and how they should be implemented. so, to sum up, we're talking about something that's being implemented for the first time. in many cases, mrs berès's remarks are very valid and correct. we all learn from this process and we evaluate its effectiveness on the basis of the results that come in to us on a daily basis, new information comes in every day, how individual countries read it and how individual countries implement the european semester. we are also seeing the results of the first discussion at eu level. the conclusions are drawn very quickly and an attempt is being made to streamline and deepen the process. at ecofin today, we made a commitment as the presidency to refer the next european commission initiatives to the relevant working groups as soon as possible, so that this process of implementing and improving the european semester can run as smoothly and as quickly as possible, to achieve the intended effect and improve the efficiency of the system and its transparency. thank you very much for your attention!
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, i am glad to address this house today on the report by mrs berès and to say that the commission welcomes the report on the european semester for economic policy coordination. i especially welcome the fact that, on a number of issues that are central to the effective and efficient delivery of the public good of economic surveillance, parliament and the commission share a common point of view. one example is the clear and shared recognition that a purely intergovernmental system of policy coordination would be inadequate to fulfil what is required of multilateral surveillance under the treaty. we need the community method for this purpose. the report also shows, to my mind, that we have a strong common understanding of the challenges that we are facing during this crisis and the direction that our response should take. it has to combine stability, growth and solidarity. the most telling example of this is the spirit of cooperation with which parliament has taken its responsibility regarding economic governance in the legislative process that led to the adoption of the six-pack legislation. the agreement between our institutions on the fundamental issues of economic policy coordination is all the more important at the present time as we face very substantial challenges for economic and financial policymaking. therefore i hope that we can repeat the success of the six-pack with regard to the new legislative proposals for further strengthening economic governance which the commission put forward last wednesday. the package of documents presented on that day reflects our commitment to closer convergence, stronger discipline and firm solidarity. on several occasions i have already stated that democratic accountability on european decision-making has to be increased – as mrs berès rightly underlined – especially if a greater degree of fiscal discipline and economic surveillance is to be conducted by the european union in relation to the member states. this is indeed extremely important and i believe that in parliament and the commission we see eye to eye on this critical matter. this is also the reason why i was – and remain – so supportive of the new economic dialogue. i look forward to our economic dialogue on the commission’s annual growth survey for 2012. this dialogue will be an excellent opportunity for parliament to express its views on the priorities for the economic agenda on growth, stability and governance. now, i recognise that not everything said in the report is necessarily flattering of how the first european semester in 2011 was conducted. i do, however, hope that you recognise that the annual growth survey for 2012 also reflects efforts on the part of the commission to take into account comments made in this house. let me conclude by saying that the introduction of the european semester in itself has been a major step forward and the 2011 experience has clearly shown improvements compared to economic surveillance done before. the six-pack will go much further and it is actually already having a practical impact because several member states are realising that they face the prospect of moving to the next step of the excessive deficit procedure, and also the possibility of financial sanctions, unless they take action in order to ensure that they meet the economic and fiscal targets of next year. i am certain that the next european semester in the first half of 2012 will be even better, that we will already have learned more lessons based on our experience this year, and that we will further improve our capacity for policymaking in a systematic manner.

in writing. − high school drop-out rates have significant socioeconomic consequences, which is why the strategy 2020 aims to reduce the drop-out rate to 10%. studies have shown that there are distinct characteristics that tend to make people more likely to miss out on their education. it is noted that girls (13%) are less likely to drop out than boys (17%). it is also clear that children from families with lower levels of qualification drop out significantly more often. migrants also have higher school dropout rates. however, this phenomenon cannot be considered in a general way, and certainly not in isolation from external factors such as poverty or abuse. evidence shows that school leavers are significantly more likely to be at risk of poverty, due in part to the lack of education and the associated opening of the labour market for such people. i am voting against the report because i believe that education and schooling are national problems for which individual solutions exist in each member state.
in writing. − high school drop-out rates have serious socioeconomic consequences: drop-outs have a negative impact on economic growth and threaten economic and social stability. if the drop-out rate across europe could be reduced by just 1% a year, it is believed that this could provide an additional half a million qualified young people. the demographic development of europe will make it particularly important to integrate as many competent young people as possible into the labour market in order to avoid being dependent on migration. i do not think the measures proposed in the report are very effective, for example, the rapporteur suggests that traditional examinations should be abolished, since this would make the grading dependent on performance on a given day. i think that traditional examination procedures are important, however, because young people also depend on them to be able to perform when they are asked to do so in their later professional and social life. i cannot agree with the rapporteur's methods and have therefore voted against the report.
in writing. − people leave early education for a variety of reasons, but their chances of entering the labour market are poor and their low income puts them at high risk of poverty. one of the six key objectives of the europe 2020 strategy is to reduce the school drop-out rate to 10% (by 2020), as the direct link between high school drop-out rates and their deceleration is clear. to achieve this objective, the eu urgently needs to put in place effective measures: the pupils must already be offered qualified assistance in vocational guidance. the current examination procedures themselves need to be reviewed and curricula adapted to the present with innovative and broad-based elements.

while the release of energy in conventional nuclear power plants is by nuclear fission, iter aims for energy by nuclear fusion. here is the crucial difference to today's nuclear power: nuclear fission releases highly toxic "radiant" substances which pose a permanent danger to man and the environment. in contrast, nuclear fusion leaves behind much less radioactive residues. iter could therefore pave the way to a sustainable energy source, even if its use for electricity generation is still a long way off. therefore, iter should be equipped with sufficient resources. europe must keep up with the times and promote forward-looking research. however, more transparency and better cost estimation are needed: exceeding the original plan by more than 300% is unacceptable! and we must not allow a steady increase in appropriations to become the norm!

in writing. − while the release of energy in conventional nuclear power plants is by nuclear fission, iter is aiming for energy from nuclear fusion. this is the crucial difference with present-day nuclear power: nuclear fission releases highly toxic 'radiant' substances which pose a permanent danger to man and the environment. in contrast, nuclear fusion leaves behind much less radioactive residues. the way forward with iter is therefore at least an optimisation of the current fission methods and an improvement on the present situation, especially for countries like austria, which for good reasons reject nuclear technology in principle. as this is an international research project, which also has to comply with international treaties, i am in principle in favour of providing it with adequate resources. it will be seen later whether iter will pave the way to a new energy source. what we urgently need is more transparency and better cost estimation: exceeding the original plan by more than 300% is unacceptable! that is why i abstained.

in writing. − the pre-accession instrument is intended to help candidate countries, such as montenegro and turkey, to prepare for accession. each year, the european court of auditors repeats the findings of irregularities and errors in the payment of pre-accession aid. in addition, the introduction of turkey should be stopped altogether, since turkey is not a suitable candidate for accession and has repeatedly and impressively demonstrated this. as in the case of turkish-occupied northern cyprus, where, despite eu aid, churches and other cultural monuments are neglected, destroyed or converted into mosques or other facilities. the report calls for greater support for the turkish community in northern cyprus, which i consider to be unacceptable in view of the situation described.
in writing. − on 17 june 2010, the european council decided to grant candidate country status to montenegro and iceland, which also entails an amendment to the regulation establishing a pre-accession facility. the second amendment, concerning article 19 on 'participation in procurement procedures and rules of origin, eligibility', takes account of member states' requests to limit participation in calls for proposals to applicants from those countries participating in the relevant ipa crossborder cooperation programmes. the third amendment, concerning article 25, ensures that the phare committee can continue to assist the commission in the management of financial assistance to the turkish cypriot community.
in writing. the fruit juice sector is a major industry worldwide. within the european union, too, this industrial sector can be attributed a not insignificant share. however, in the case of fruit juice production, especially the popular orange juice, 80% of the volume consumed in the eu is imported from north america and brazil. the production process is also different, since in these countries all fruit is used for juice processing, but in the eu only the waste products that are no longer needed for trade. for the consumer, this means that the origin of the juice must be indicated in a particularly clear way in order to be able to tell him unequivocally where his product comes from. in general, the labelling of the ingredients of juices is not insignificant, especially as regards flavourings and sugar additives. consumers are also frequently confused by the terms 'juice' and 'nectar'. i voted in favour of the report because i agree with the rapporteur that clear labelling is essential for the good of consumers.
in writing. - in the fruit juice sector, there are varieties which are imported to over 80%, for example from brazil or the usa. for citrus fruit, the european industry is an auxiliary industry complementary to fresh processing, in contrast to large international producers. the processing is often used to sell fruit which, because of its appearance (size, spots) is not marketed as fresh fruit, although it is quite suitable for producing high-quality fruit juices. due to the high environmental costs of imports (co2 emissions), it is of key importance to strengthen the european fruit juice industry. this would also prevent the destruction of less fruit suitable for fresh sale and prevent unharvested fruit from rotting in the field, which can lead to the spread of diseases. this creates socioeconomic added value by creating jobs and growth. the commission will also be seeking clarifications on labelling, classification, authorised ingredients and practices. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive. this will create an incentive for third countries to improve the quality of their products by using more sustainable production methods. the commission has also adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of consumers in the event of the use of certain substances in foodstuffs. the report, which takes account of these aspects, has my vote.
in writing. - there is an urgent need to improve consumer information on the content of fruit juices, in particular on sugar content. in particular, consumer groups with special needs (children, diabetics, people with weight problems) need to be protected from possible misinformation and misleading. the european citrus processing industry should also be encouraged by bringing the directive into line with international standards. in addition to economic benefits and job creation, strengthening the european citrus sector reduces the high environmental costs of carbon-intensive imports of citrus from overseas.
in writing. − phosphorus, mainly from household products such as dishwashing detergents and detergents, is a major contributor to the pollution of european waters. phosphate entering the water creates a good breeding ground for algae and other aquatic plants, which in turn leads to the depletion of additional oxygen in the water, which other organisms such as fish need to survive. this can lead to the extinction of species in the long term, which would cause considerable damage to ecosystems. the commission is now considering regulatory measures to encourage manufacturers of phosphorus-containing detergents to reduce the substance. i voted in favour of the report because i agree with the rapporteur that dishwashers should also be included in the proposal, since they are now almost a standard household item, like washing machines.
in writing. − household products such as dishwashing or laundry detergents contain phosphorus. this substance hardens the water and thus allows for more efficient purification. however, phosphorus can have a massive negative impact when it enters our domestic waters, such as rivers or lakes. the situation is particularly serious in the danube basin. the problem is that phosphorus promotes the growth of algae and other aquatic plants, which in turn deprives the water of oxygen, which is essential for fish and other animals to survive. in the medium and long term, phosphorus pollution threatens to extinguish many fish and aquatic species; the ecological balance of the waters is disturbed. the present proposal aims at reducing the proportion of phosphorus in budgetary appropriations, including, in any event, the provision for dishwashing detergents. that is why i voted in favour.
in writing. the aim of this proposal for a regulation is to establish a maximum level for phosphorus in household detergents. the background is that phosphorus in detergents and dishwashing detergents is currently responsible for a large part of the pollution of our waters. while there are already phosphate-free liquid detergents which are increasingly gaining market share, there is currently no alternative on the market for dishwashers and it is therefore recommended that a fixed date be included in the phosphorus limitation regulation to provide incentives for the necessary innovation. i agreed to it.
in writing. − the fisheries agreement with morocco is not only expensive and a source of international concern, but also inefficient: although the principles of sustainability in socioeconomic and environmental terms should also apply outside the territorial waters of the member states and the eu, unfortunately, this is not the case. the eu's large fisheries organisations are also failing to represent the interests of small-scale fishermen adequately and are bidding for large international groups. i therefore voted against this report.
in writing. − the fisheries agreement with morocco, which is to give 11 eu member states access to fishing grounds in moroccan territorial waters, is due to be renewed. the evaluation of the last four years of the agreement showed that the objectives were not met. the eu's aim of stabilising the fisheries market has not been achieved, and the large flow of money from the eu to morocco for fisheries has brought only a slight improvement in the situation of fishermen. there are also serious concerns about emerging environmental problems and a conflict of international law situation. i have refused because of the many and great concerns.
in writing. − uncoordinated cuts in defence budgets by most eu member states as a result of the crisis have the potential to make the eu unable to meet its international security responsibilities in terms of peacekeeping and conflict prevention. the report calls for the replacement of isolated national defence planning by constructive dialogue. i have agreed with the report as a whole.
in writing. - the eu is continuing to pursue democracy-building under the guise of fighting terrorism. the eu has made a small contribution to the transfer of counter-terrorism data to the us. the united states has also targeted individual member states, put them under pressure and blackmailed them into giving up or accessing all sorts of data - a data protection disaster. and this, although it is still not proven that this wealth of information can guarantee the success in the fight against terrorism that is used as a justification for the circumvention of basic fundamental rights. instead of spying on all eu citizens, the eu should once again focus on fighting the flourishing organised crime and pushing forward security-critical projects such as the schengen information system. the proposed measures, which seem to lead to the blacklisting of anyone who does not share the views of the mainstream media, must be rejected.
in writing. − under the guise of fighting international terrorism, the us is putting pressure on the eu and its member states to release data. in principle, all eu citizens are placed under general suspicion, rather than specific data on individuals where there is a stronger suspicion. moreover, it has not been demonstrated that the transmission of data in bulk is actually used for the purpose of combating terrorism. the report is a restriction on data protection, civil rights and freedom of expression and must therefore be rejected.

member of the commission. − madam president, i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr geier, for his contribution to the effectiveness and efficiency of eu development assistance in afghanistan. the commission shares the view that our commitment to afghanistan must focus on the long-term perspective. at the bonn conference on 5 december 2011 the eu looked to the afghan government to provide the context for this long-term engagement by improving governance and the rule of law and making other structural reforms which are necessary for the transformation of afghanistan into a fully-functioning, sustainable state at the service of its people. in bonn the eu and its member states also announced the negotiation of a partnership agreement on cooperation and development with afghanistan. this agreement will create a coherent, legally-binding overall framework for eu relations with afghanistan. this long-term commitment will be conditional on the afghan government’s progress in further strengthening public finance management systems, reducing corruption, improving budget execution, developing a financing strategy and increasing government capacity. the establishment of a fully independent control and audit office will also remain a precondition for budget support. as the afghan government progressively takes over full responsibility for security and development, we also expect democratic institutions to be strengthened both at central and provincial level. in this context the commission will continue to assist afghanistan by ensuring that monitoring mechanisms adequately address corruption and proper management of aid and that the recipient communities are involved in identifying needs and shaping development assistance policies. shortcomings of external assistance in afghanistan are the result of a complex mix of political factors, military insurgency, economic underdevelopment and drug trafficking, to name just a few. in this environment, multi-donor trust funds have been instrumental in pooling donors around afghan-owned strategies, harmonising aid and contributing to strengthening national public finance management capacities. they also enable the efficient donor division of labour and facilitate pooling donors’ specific expertise and resources. the eu aims to surpass the goal of providing 50% of development assistance either directly (on budget) or through multi-donor trust funds, as agreed within the kabul process. in buzan earlier this month the commission reiterated its commitment towards aid effectiveness, focusing and deepening on results and accountability, ownership, transparency and reduced fragmentation of aid. this is also our commitment to afghanistan. with 2014 on the horizon, we will need to focus on reinforcing current mechanisms to ensure that afghanistan becomes a fully-functioning and sustainable state capable of fighting fraud and corruption.
i have to say, madam president, i have read the report, of course. we have already invested more than eur 2 billion in afghanistan from the european union between 2002 and 2010. i think the report comes to a very clear conclusion: there is a high level of corruption, a lack of administrative capacity, a high risk of waste, no independent control bodies, projects without sustainability and effectiveness, and unrealistic timing of projects. in my view, we as the budgetary control authority cannot guarantee to the european taxpayers that the money in afghanistan is being used economically and sustainably. we cannot guarantee that these problems will be solved in the medium term. that is why i have come to a different conclusion from some of my colleagues, namely that we should end this armed development aid to afghanistan as soon as possible.

in writing. − the eu committee on budgetary control has decided to examine in more detail the management of eu funds in afghanistan. the result of this evaluation was that enormous deficiencies were found. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union-wide network of national and regional authorities responsible for the implementation of the eu's external action. from this analysis he concludes that the future method should be "direct budgetary aid to the afghan state budget" - i do not agree with this. the rapporteur acknowledges the problem of vulnerability to fraud and corruption, but believes that the clause allowing badly functioning administrations to withdraw budgetary aid is a sufficient countermeasure. the obligation to provide accounts is not sufficiently met and the actual assistance provided by the individual is at best only mediocre. the disadvantages of 'joint management with international organisations' are not easy to overcome: it should be clear that ngos that receive eu funds for management should provide clear and unambiguous periodic accounts of what has been spent and how much has been spent, and these reports should also be published on the institutions' website.
in writing. − the expectations expressed in the report regarding further improvements in the egf's procedure and the call for a higher level of efficiency and transparency and for better visibility of the fund are welcome. in times of economic uncertainty, it is all the more important to be able to help those people who have lost their jobs as a result of the current financial and economic crisis. the improvements required should enable the fund to provide more targeted and rapid interventions in the future. efficient use of assistance for areas with high unemployment is essential. finally, it would be fatal if people who have become unemployed could not be helped as quickly as possible because of a lengthy egf procedure. i therefore support the demands and expectations set out in the report. i therefore gave my consent.
